What is $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}?$ 

![](images/bd/bd2cf58c26a51ae147b3714556631e1df786ae6e56cde01f801d9d93f7c258f5.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124496 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f0cfdcd8-92d0-5768-aa59-2dc769427d08" "question-2be7f5e5-3b31-5fb7-85df-a4fc0339bd35"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124309 :question/problem "The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ to $\mathcal{C} = \{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$ is given below. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ given that $\mathbf{x} =2\mathbf{c}_1-6\mathbf{c}_2.$

![](images/15/15e0d0c04e0352356acab8001936031505931dac7eb7afefa1881dd333448e57.svg)" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} .
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-4)(-4)-6\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -3 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & \frac{3}{2} \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $\mathbf{x} = 2 \mathbf{c}_1-6\mathbf{c}_2,$ we obtain
![](images/17/178769437e55f1822723ac4cc090efca62aac6be9e3ad9dc8f7971b8a6196484.svg)

Now, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & \frac{3}{2} \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124497 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-15cdd9a6-5092-51ed-93a5-b2dd11d2ff12"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124310 :question/problem "The basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}$ are given below. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$

![](images/0b/0b395052cc098a6daeb50037d07223b20fb93163c10c31a432c7fb9c9a7804db.svg)" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} .
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}.$ As a result, we have

![](images/82/82e477164a2708a6f8e7f1142dce3e290d3aa216b5828e0523c16555533f02b7.svg)

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 10-3\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124577 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ef5b0192-0a59-538e-b7e8-f10e0dd5b78e" "question-e28dac56-d247-5873-8ab6-f1ab402c91a9" "question-e6749d20-907b-5109-a739-bd517d7b2b94"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124384 :question/problem "The bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}$ are given below. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}.$ 

![](images/c6/c61cc387c58af544cf95641a1c2a28e5412d223fb03a7afe5157ee4eba3902bb.svg)" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \},$ respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

So, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix
![](images/76/76d9c82037008323681ec9a0745b39740bf1405c767fc9aaee411cdd1fadde1a.svg)

Reducing the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 6 & 13 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-6){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 11 & 15 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$ is
![](images/48/481e6321dd23a8af4c59201685295862cc927731eeec31c122ec62bdf156d179.svg)

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}[\,x\,]_{B} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}11 & 15 \\ -5 & -7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-7fe8ffd2-b435-528e-b48e-7a1540a8e35d" :question/id #uuid "7fe8ffd2-b435-528e-b48e-7a1540a8e35d" :question/math-academy-id "q-113559" :question/problem "The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B$ to the basis $C$ and the coordinates of the vector $x$ relative to the basis $B$ are given below. What is $[x]_{C}?$ 

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}],\,[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -6\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "Given the coordinates of $x$ relative to $B$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C,$ we find the coordinates of $x$ relative to $C$ as follows:

$$

Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=4{c}_{1}+6{c}_{2}.$ 

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 6-7\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}6 & -7 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{7}{3} \\ -1 & \frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=4{c}_{1}+6{c}_{2},$ we obtain  

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{7}{3} \\ -1 & \frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5d503694-4c65-5f5e-80a7-c8e1b24fe6d1"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Suppose that $\mathbf x \in V$ for some vector space $V,$ and that $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ are two bases of $V.$ 

To find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to $\mathcal B,$ we can use the **change-of-basis formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [\,x\,]_{B},\end{aligned}
$$

where we recall that

- $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ and $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}$ are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ respectively, and

- $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of vectors of the basis $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

As an example, suppose we are given two bases $\mathcal{B}=\left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\}$ of a vector space $V,$ and we already know that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by
![](images/d9/d9388f46f84cc0c6b1d7e5cf43ee973085366ae4f44cfe74515c59bfc1994662.svg)

Let $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and ![](images/f9/f99f37621c20057077eb7c6e23690a45159cfe1b665c6b88b4a604f8687728bf.svg) Then we can easily find $[\,\mathbf{v}\,]_{\mathcal{C}},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,v\,]_{C} & =\overset{{P}_{B\to C}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot \overset{[v]_{B}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125822 :tutorial/content "We've seen that to find the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to a basis $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to a basis $\mathcal B,$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [\,x\,]_{B}.\end{aligned}
$$

In expanded form, the formula looks as follows:
![](images/89/890f34433211786e2cb8aa71057de40bdf3b12678c2bbb5a79ef5e680555937f.svg)

Also, remember that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ and from $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ to $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ are the inverses of each other:

$$
P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}
	\quad\textrm{and}\quad
	P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125708 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$ be bases of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Now, suppose we would like to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ 

- We first need to find $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that 

$$
x_1 \mathbf{c}_1+x_2 \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_1,
$$

which is equivalent to solving the system with the augmented matrix
![](images/58/58010a2a5206e3fc27e3d924de70cf32dcc92c3578bdb2821ace7278fbb223cf.svg)

- Similarly, we need to find $y_1$ and $y_2$ such that 

$$
y_1 \mathbf{c}_1+y_2 \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_2,
$$

which is equivalent to solving the system with the augmented matrix
![](images/68/68788aa3e388c5cba14662a947c1b7afaacb95f611c256d11a7a6d7614c352b9.svg)

We can solve both systems using Gaussian elimination. However, we can do that simultaneously by considering the matrix
![](images/4b/4b00a4cbd7831f6da6acd06a087d5453bd455a89eb81f6b3036b1b572bb064d1.svg)

Reducing the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination, we get a matrix of the form

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & {x}_{1} & {y}_{1} \\ 0 & 1 & {x}_{2} & {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where the required coefficients will be stored in the columns on the right-hand side." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124710 :activity/expected-seconds 1080.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ given that $\mathbf{x} =2\mathbf{c}_1-6\mathbf{c}_2.$

![](images/15/15e0d0c04e0352356acab8001936031505931dac7eb7afefa1881dd333448e57.svg)" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} .
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-4)(-4)-6\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -3 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & \frac{3}{2} \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $\mathbf{x} = 2 \mathbf{c}_1-6\mathbf{c}_2,$ we obtain
![](images/17/178769437e55f1822723ac4cc090efca62aac6be9e3ad9dc8f7971b8a6196484.svg)

Now, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & \frac{3}{2} \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124497 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-15cdd9a6-5092-51ed-93a5-b2dd11d2ff12"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124310 :question/problem "The basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}$ are given below. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$

![](images/0b/0b395052cc098a6daeb50037d07223b20fb93163c10c31a432c7fb9c9a7804db.svg)" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} .
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}.$ As a result, we have

![](images/82/82e477164a2708a6f8e7f1142dce3e290d3aa216b5828e0523c16555533f02b7.svg)

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 10-3\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 6-7\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}6 & -7 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{7}{3} \\ -1 & \frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=4{c}_{1}+6{c}_{2},$ we obtain  

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{7}{3} \\ -1 & \frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 16 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 13 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}13 & 6 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}13 & 6 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

"Suppose that $\mathbf x \in V$ for some vector space $V,$ and that $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ are two bases of $V.$ 

To find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to $\mathcal B,$ we can use the **change-of-basis formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [\,x\,]_{B},\end{aligned}
$$

where we recall that

- $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ and $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}$ are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ respectively, and

- $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of vectors of the basis $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

As an example, suppose we are given two bases $\mathcal{B}=\left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\}$ of a vector space $V,$ and we already know that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by
![](images/d9/d9388f46f84cc0c6b1d7e5cf43ee973085366ae4f44cfe74515c59bfc1994662.svg)

Let $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and ![](images/f9/f99f37621c20057077eb7c6e23690a45159cfe1b665c6b88b4a604f8687728bf.svg) Then we can easily find $[\,\mathbf{v}\,]_{\mathcal{C}},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,v\,]_{C} & =\overset{{P}_{B\to C}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot \overset{[v]_{B}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125822 :tutorial/content "We've seen that to find the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to a basis $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to a basis $\mathcal B,$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [\,x\,]_{B}.\end{aligned}
$$

In expanded form, the formula looks as follows:
![](images/89/890f34433211786e2cb8aa71057de40bdf3b12678c2bbb5a79ef5e680555937f.svg)

Also, remember that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ and from $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ to $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ are the inverses of each other:

$$
P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}
	\quad\textrm{and}\quad
	P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125708 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$ be bases of $\mathbb{R}^2.$ Now, suppose we would like to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ 

- We first need to find $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that 

$$
x_1 \mathbf{c}_1+x_2 \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_1,
$$

which is equivalent to solving the system with the augmented matrix
![](images/58/58010a2a5206e3fc27e3d924de70cf32dcc92c3578bdb2821ace7278fbb223cf.svg)

- Similarly, we need to find $y_1$ and $y_2$ such that 

$$
y_1 \mathbf{c}_1+y_2 \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_2,
$$

which is equivalent to solving the system with the augmented matrix
![](images/68/68788aa3e388c5cba14662a947c1b7afaacb95f611c256d11a7a6d7614c352b9.svg)

We can solve both systems using Gaussian elimination. However, we can do that simultaneously by considering the matrix

Reducing the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination, we get a matrix of the form

$$

:question/problem "The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ to $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=4{c}_{1}+6{c}_{2}.$ 

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$"] ["question-f0cfdcd8-92d0-5768-aa59-2dc769427d08" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 7 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 6-7\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}6 & -7 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{7}{3} \\ -1 & \frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=4{c}_{1}+6{c}_{2},$ we obtain  

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -\frac{7}{3} \\ -1 & \frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-f0cfdcd8-92d0-5768-aa59-2dc769427d08" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-5d503694-4c65-5f5e-80a7-c8e1b24fe6d1" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S}.
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $B$ relative to the standard basis $S.$ As a result, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{S\to B}$ from $S$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{7\cdot 2-3\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}2 & -5 \\ -3 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ 3 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ 3 & -7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-15cdd9a6-5092-51ed-93a5-b2dd11d2ff12" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-61a8f832-f2b3-5123-8233-870da3bb21e1" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 16 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 13 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}13 & 6 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}13 & 6 \\ -4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ef5b0192-0a59-538e-b7e8-f10e0dd5b78e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-4b4d2688-b184-5811-a90b-5873e7a47367" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-4)(-4)-6\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -3 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & \frac{3}{2} \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.

$$

$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}22 \\ 35\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

:question/problem "The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ to $C={{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$ is given below. Find $[x]_{B}$ given that $x=5{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}.$

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}5 & 10 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,x\,]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C}.
$$

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ from $C$ to $B.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}5 & 10 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 5-2\cdot 10}[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -\frac{2}{5} & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that since $x=5{c}_{1}-{c}_{2},$ we obtain

$$
[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -\frac{2}{5} & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124497 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124310 :question/id #uuid "a2d3629f-5b7c-5b65-998f-8754ff11e7b7" :question/math-academy-id "e-4841"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7f58bd46-07f7-54a5-8499-5e4e3515b610" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124993 :question/id #uuid "9b5f682f-a0de-52f6-930d-b54c3a22eede" :question/math-academy-id "q-36488"} {:db/id 17592186125036 :question/id #uuid "618e1711-d591-5872-b815-9d14ad33b674" :question/math-academy-id "q-37160"} {:db/id 17592186247377 :question/id #uuid "ca416b56-0c6d-5fb5-8b76-d2124cfd2e38" :question/math-academy-id "q-113600"} {:db/id 17592186247379 :question/id #uuid "162a4f62-2177-5623-998d-5746dbddde07" :question/math-academy-id "q-113606"} {:db/id 17592186351453 :question/id #uuid "5ee6ca5a-3bdd-5fec-a9fa-7000d4a0cb6f" :question/math-academy-id "q-82710"} {:db/id 17592186394414 :question/id #uuid "5c7d63da-59ab-5308-9b89-bf650fb9db9b" :question/math-academy-id "q-82606"} {:db/id 17592186394421 :question/id #uuid "13aef9df-8682-5fe0-a906-e0817933e236" :question/math-academy-id "q-82609"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in the Standard Basis"} {:db/id 17592186124310 :question/id #uuid "a2d3629f-5b7c-5b65-998f-8754ff11e7b7" :question/math-academy-id "e-4841" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186124497 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7f58bd46-07f7-54a5-8499-5e4e3515b610" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in the Standard Basis"}] :question/problem "The basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}$ are given below. ![](images/0d/0dcc93449ac1d14e51850e4a74f639aeb3acd21b720ba2b9deeb2208d9fffeb4.png)" :question/worked-solution "We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

$$
[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} .
$$

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}.$ As a result, we have

![](images/50/50bbd2dd0fa1c0732a01d07c2614ab15549272fcc0b7d686651f0464b3b50f39.png)

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{S\to B} & ={P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 10\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 10-3\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{S\to B}[\,x\,]_{S} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186124993 :question/id #uuid "9b5f682f-a0de-52f6-930d-b54c3a22eede" :question/math-academy-id "q-36488" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124497 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7f58bd46-07f7-54a5-8499-5e4e3515b610" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis Given Its Coordinates in the Standard Basis"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1dcd4ef1-4949-58ef-aa67-9540954fdc1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186321374} {:answer/id #uuid "41ecfd30-c58f-5e8b-8238-dbc9493bac67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186321670} {:answer/id #uuid "46420e90-1c10-5b3a-a995-8806f1bcee0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186321702} {:answer/id #uuid "6e560467-13af-562b-ad43-d89f3b3f3260" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186322002} {:answer/id #uuid "d1bf20ff-37e7-5af1-a632-1f6b46091107" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186322785}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "46420e90-1c10-5b3a-a995-8806f1bcee0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186321702} :answer-field/id #uuid "4370689f-d468-5230-a5de-f45535b13a11" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186323298}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$

$$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 3 & -2 \\ 3 & 10 & 4 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 18 & -29 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ is

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}18 & -29 \\ -5 & 9\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we compute $[\,x\,]_{B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}[\,x\,]_{C} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & -29 \\ -5 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-11 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

:topic/math-academy-id 1910} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125361 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125768 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf x \in V$ for some vector space $V,$ and that $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ are two bases of $V.$ 

To find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to $\mathcal B,$ we can use the **change-of-basis formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [\,x\,]_{B},\end{aligned}
$$

where we recall that

- $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ and $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}$ are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ respectively, and

- $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of vectors of the basis $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

As an example, suppose we are given two bases $\mathcal{B}=\left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\}$ of a vector space $V,$ and we already know that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Let $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and $[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ Then we can easily find $[\,\mathbf{v}\,]_{\mathcal{C}},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,v\,]_{C} & =\overset{{P}_{B\to C}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot \overset{[v]_{B}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "827e9581-9fde-5941-ad91-2c364796e5b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3217 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "910841a1-0516-546a-8aac-f188c965b763" :step/math-academy-id {:db/id 17592186125500 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125822 :tutorial/content "We've seen that to find the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to a basis $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to a basis $\mathcal B,$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [\,x\,]_{B}.\end{aligned}
$$

In expanded form, the formula looks as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}| \\ [x]_{C} \\ |\end{aligned}
$$

Also, remember that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ and from $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ to $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ are the inverses of each other:

$$
P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}
	\quad\textrm{and}\quad
	P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1}

$$
x_1 \mathbf{c}_1+x_2 \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_1,

which is equivalent to solving the system with the augmented matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}| & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} \\ | & | & |\end{aligned}

$$
y_1 \mathbf{c}_1+y_2 \mathbf{c}_2 = \mathbf{b}_2,

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}
$$

$$

where the required coefficients will be stored in the columns on the right-hand side." :tutorial/id #uuid "d42ee304-2e1f-5cc2-b334-65d083ea7323" :tutorial/math-academy-id 13287 :tutorial/title "Using Gaussian Elimination to Find the Coordinates of a Vector in a New Basis"} :step/id #uuid "184b8c31-de1a-5e34-ad87-2f626c830182" :step/math-academy-id 462199 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125498}}] :activity/title "Changing a Basis Using the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124710} {:db/id 17592186125361 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125768 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf x \in V$ for some vector space $V,$ and that $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ are two bases of $V.$ 

To find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{C}$ given its coordinates relative to $\mathcal B,$ we can use the **change-of-basis formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,x\,]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [\,x\,]_{B},\end{aligned}
$$

where we recall that

- $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ and $[\,\mathbf x\,]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}$ are the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ respectively, and

- $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of vectors of the basis $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

As an example, suppose we are given two bases $\mathcal{B}=\left\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2 \right\}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\left\{ \mathbf{c}_1, \mathbf{c}_2 \right\}$ of a vector space $V,$ and we already know that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Let $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and $[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ Then we can easily find $[\,\mathbf{v}\,]_{\mathcal{C}},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\,v\,]_{C} & =\overset{{P}_{B\to C}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot \overset{[v]_{B}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "827e9581-9fde-5941-ad91-2c364796e5b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3217 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "910841a1-0516-546a-8aac-f188c965b763" :step/math-academy-id 17537 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125500}} {:db/id 17592186125768 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf x \in V$ for some vector space $V,$ and that $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ are two bases of $V.$

17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.
Students learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating
